ingredients.item: Firm white fish fillet (cod or halibut)

instructions: Scrub the mussels under cold water. Pull off any stringy beard by tugging it toward the hinge. Tap any open mussel on the counter. If it doesn't close, throw it out. Put the mussels in a bowl in the fridge.
Quarter the fennel, cut out the core and slice it thinly. Thinly slice the onion and the garlic.
Heat the olive oil in a large heavy pot over medium heat. Add the onion, fennel and 1/4 tsp of the salt. Cook for 8 minutes, stirring now and then, until soft but not brown.
Add the garlic, bay leaf, thyme and oregano. Cook for 1 minute, stirring, until it smells fragrant.
Add 1 tbsp of the tomato paste and stir for 1 minute, until it darkens a shade.
Add the wine and the clam juice. Bring to a simmer and cook for 5 minutes, scraping up anything stuck to the bottom of the pot.
Add the tomatoes with their juice, crushing each one against the side of the pot with a wooden spoon. Cover with the lid slightly open, lower the heat and simmer for 20 minutes.
Meanwhile, pat the shrimp and fish dry. Cut the fish into 2 inch pieces. Sprinkle the shrimp and fish with the pepper and the remaining 1/2 tsp salt. Chop the parsley until you have about 2 tbsp.
Add the mussels to the pot, cover and cook for 4 minutes, until they start to open.
Add the shrimp, then lay the fish pieces on top. Cover and cook for 4 to 5 minutes, until the shrimp are pink and curled and the fish is opaque and flakes when you press it.
Fish the bay leaf out and throw it away, along with any mussels that didn't open.
Take the pot off the heat. Add the butter and the parsley and stir gently until the butter melts. Stir slowly so the fish stays in pieces.
Taste it. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
Ladle into wide bowls. Serve with the crusty bread and the red pepper flakes on the table.
method_notes: Coley Cooks (the lead) sweats onion and fennel, cooks the garlic and herbs, stirs in tomato paste, adds wine and clam juice, simmers the tomatoes for 20 minutes, and adds the shellfish first and the fish last. Well Seasoned Studio builds a shrimp-shell stock first and uses fennel seed, but is the same stew underneath. This one follows the lead and trims it to the three seafoods in the dish note: mussels, shrimp and fish, dropping the clams and crab so it is an easier shop. The chili flakes move to the table to keep the pot mild. Only two versions were readable, and Well Seasoned Studio shows no rating.
